questions.q_en: Who was the founder of the Mauryan Empire?
questions.solution_en:
• Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Mauryan Empire.

Further Insight:

• Chandragupta Maurya (321 BCE - 297 BCE)

○ According to Parishishtaparvan by Hemachandra, Chandragupta was the grandson of the chief of the peacock tamers clan (mayura-poshakas).

○ Chandragupta established the vast Mauryan Empire.

○ His empire included Bihar, Nepal, western and north-western India, and parts of the Deccan.

○ In 305 BCE, Chandragupta annexed regions in the Hindu Kush, previously ruled by satraps appointed by Alexander.

■ Seleucus Nicator launched a campaign to reclaim these areas.

■ Treaty with Seleucus (303 BCE)

■ Seleucus ceded territories:

• Arachosia (Kandahar, Afghanistan)

• Gedrosia (South Baluchistan)

• Paropamisadai (Afghanistan-Indian border)

■ The treaty recognized intermarriage rights between Greeks and Indians.

○ Megasthenes and Dionysius resided at Chandragupta's court.

○ Chandragupta abdicated the throne and became a Jain disciple under Bhadrabahu.

questions.q_en: Who was the ambassador of Selcus Nicator in Chandragupta Maurya court?
questions.solution_en:
• Magasthenes was the ambassador of Sekcus Nicator in Chandragupta Maurya Court.

Further Insight:

• Megasthenes

○ Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya in Pataliputra (modern-day Patna).

○ Indica

■ Indica' is Megasthenes' account of his observations during his stay in India

■ Detailed descriptions of India's landscape, rivers, and cities.

■ Insights into the caste system, customs, and daily life.

■ Information on governance, military, and economy.

■ Observations on Indian philosophical thought and religious practices.

○ 'Indica' serves as a crucial source for understanding ancient India from a foreign perspective

○ The original text is lost, fragments preserved by later writers like Strabo, Arrian, and Diodorus have been instrumental in reconstructing India's history.

questions.q_en: Which Mauryan Emperor was referred to as Amitrochates by the Greeks?
questions.solution_en:
• Bindusara referred to as Amitrochates by the Greek Sources

• Mahabhasya(Written by Patanjali) refers Bindusara as Amitraghata( A slayer of enemies)

Further Insight:

• Bindusara (297 BCE - 273 BCE)

○ Bindusara was referred to as Amitraghata (Slayer of Enemies) in the Mahabhashya written by Patanjali

■ Greek sources mention him as Amitrochates.

○ Bindusara brought sixteen states under the Mauryan Empire.

○ He conquered the land between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.

○ His southern expansion extended into the Deccan region, stopping near modern-day Karnataka.

○ Deimachus, an ambassador from Seleucid emperor Antiochus I, resided at Bindusara's court.

○ Bindusara was associated with the Ajivika sect, a religious tradition prominent during the Mauryan period.

questions.q_en: Which Sect Bindusara joined?
questions.solution_en:
• Bindusara joined Ajivika Sect.

Further Insight:

• Ajivika Sect

○ Makkhali Gosāla, a contemporary of Mahavira and Gautama Buddha, established the Ājīvika sect in the 5th century BCE.

○ Ājīvikas believed that all events are predetermined by fate (niyati), rendering human effort and free will ineffective.

○ They dismissed the concept of karma influencing future outcomes, viewing life's course as fixed.

○ The sect did not acknowledge a creator god.

○ Emperor Bindusara, the second Mauryan ruler, is believed to have been a follower of the Ājīvika tradition.

○ The Barabar Caves in Bihar, associated with the Ājīvikas, stand as enduring monuments to their historical presence.

questions.q_en: While Bindusara was Emperor, Ashoka was appointed as Viceroy of ________ and ________.
questions.solution_en:
• While Bindusara was Emperor, Ashoka was appointed as Viceroy of Taxila and Ujjain

Further InsightL:

• Ashoka (272 BCE - 232 BCE)

○ Appointed as Viceroy of Taxila and Ujjain during his father Bindusara's reign.

○ Ashoka was the first ruler to establish direct contact with his people through inscriptions.

○ He was also known as the Buddhashakya, Dharmasoka, Devanampiya, Piyadassi etc..

○ There were five provinces described in inscriptions of Ashoka i.e.

■ (1) Uttarapath

■ (2) Avantiratha

■ (3) Kalinga

■ (4) Dakshinapath

■ (5) Prachyapatha

○ Kalinga War

■ Kalinga was a prosperous, free region with significant ports and a strong navy.

■ Kalinga controlled the land and sea routes to South India. The territory of Kalinga was like a bridge between north and south

■ The 13th rock edict provides evidence of the Kalinga war

■ Witnessing immense loss of life, Ashoka renounced violence and embraced peace.

○ Became a Buddhist proponent and organized the 3rd Buddhist Council at Pataliputra.

○ Dhamma: Derived from 'Dharma,' it was not tied to any specific religion but promoted ethical principles.

○ Edicts: Explained the principles of Dhamma across his empire.

questions.q_en: Kautilya serves as Minister under which Mauryan Ruler?
questions.solution_en:
• Kautilya also known as Chankya and Vishnugupta served as Prime Minister, advisor and Chief Priest in the court of Chandragupta Maurya.

Further Insight:

• Kautilya (Chanakya or Vishnugupta)

○ Kautilya, also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta, was a Brahmin scholar and statesman.

○ Served as Prime Minister, chief advisor and chief priest to Chandragupta Maurya, founder of the Mauryan Empire.

○ Arthashastra

■ Comprehensive treatise on statecraft, economic policy, military strategy, and governance.

■ Considered a foundational text in political science and economics in ancient India.

○ Advocated pragmatic and sometimes ruthless policies for rulers to maintain power and stability.

○ Kautilya's ideas have been compared to those of Machiavelli, highlighting his contributions to political realism.

questions.q_en: Ashoka the Mauryan ruler built Sanchi Stupa, which is also a UNESCO cultural heritage site. What is the location of Sachi Stupa?
questions.solution_en:
• Sanchi Stupa is located in the Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh

Further Insight:

• Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi

○ Sanchi, near Vidisha in central India, located on a forested plateau.

○ Sanchi documents the evolution of Buddhism from the 3rd century BCE to the 12th century CE.

○ Mentioned as Cetiyagiri in Sri Lankan chronicles, where Mahindra, son of Emperor Ashoka, stopped before his mission to Sri Lanka.

○ Sanchi Stupa

■ Initially built by Ashoka (3rd century BCE) with a monolithic pillar (Aśoka Stambha).

■ Expanded during the Sunga dynasty with stone veneer, staircases, harmika, yashti, and chhatra.

■ Satavahana dynasty (1st century CE) added four toranas (gateways).

■ Gupta dynasty (5th century CE) built shrines at cardinal points.

○ Known for Aniconic Art: Buddha depicted symbolically (e.g., footprints, lotus).

○ Bas-relief and high-relief sculptures illustrate Jataka stories and Buddhist teachings.

○ Represents integration of indigenous and non-indigenous artistic traditions.

○ Contains remains of Buddha's disciples Sariputra and Maudgalyayana.

○ Served as a major Buddhist center until the 13th century CE.

•

questions.q_en: Who was the last Mauryan ruler assassinated by his Brahmin General Pushyamitra Shunga?
questions.solution_en:
• Brihadratha was the last ruler of the Mauryan Empire and was assassinated by his Brahmin General Pushyamitra Shunga.

Further Insight:

• Brihadratha (187 BCE - 185 BCE)

○ Brihadratha was the final ruler of the Mauryan dynasty.

○ He was assassinated by Pushyamitra Shunga, his Brahman commander-in-chief, who later founded the Shunga Empire.

• Reasons for the Decline of the Mauryan Empire

○ After Ashoka's death (232 BCE), the empire experienced a rapid succession of short-reigning rulers.

○ These rulers failed to establish stable governance, leading to weakened imperial control.

○ The Dhamma-mahamattas (state officials) grew too powerful and oppressive in the later years of Ashoka's reign.

○ Weak rulers resulted in a proliferation of officials loyal only to the king, rather than the state.

○ The collapse of the spy network contributed to corruption and inefficiency.

○ Erosion of state monopolies on metals, particularly iron, affected the economy.

○ Environmental issues like deforestation and floods, along with famines (e.g., in North Bengal), further weakened the empire.

○ The centralised taxation system led to economic difficulties, with suggestions in Arthashastra to tax even actors and prostitutes to boost revenue.
